source_text: Procedente oratione postulamus et dicimus: panem nostrum cottidianum da nobis hodie. quod potest et spiritaliter et simpliciter intellegi, quia et uterque intellectus utilitate diuina proficit ad salutem. nam panis uitae Christus est et panis hic omnium non est, sed noster est. et quomodo dicimus pater noster, quia intellegentium et credentium pater est, sic et panem nostrum uocamus, quia Christus eorum qui corpus eius contingimus panis est. hunc autem panem dari nobis cottidie postulamus, ne qui in Christo sumus et eucharistiam eius cottidie ad cibum salutis accipimus intercedente aliquo grauiore delicto, dum abstenti et non communicantes a caelesti pane prohibemur, a Christi corpore separemur ipso praedicante et dicente: ego sum panis uitae qui de caelo descendi. si qui ederit de meo pane, uiuet in aeternum. panem autem quem ego dedero caro mea est pro saeculi uita. quando ergo dicit in aeternum uiuere si qui ederit de eius pane, ut manifestum est eos uiuere qui corpus eius adtingunt et eucharistiam iure communicationis accipiunt, ita contra timendum est et orandum, ne dum quis abstentus separatur a Christi corpore remaneat a salute comminante ipso et dicente: nisi ederitis carnem filii hominis et biberitis sanguinem eius, non habebitis uitam in uobis. et ideo panem nostrum id est Christum dari nobis cottidie petimus, ut qui in Christo manemus et uiuimus a sanctificatione eius et corpore non recedamus.
thought_title: Daily bread as Christ and the Eucharist
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the petition 'give us this day our daily bread' in the Lord's Prayer, first in its spiritual sense as Christ received in the Eucharist.
pass_a_gloss: Proceeding [with] prayer we ask and we say: bread our daily give [to] us today. which can both spiritually and simply be understood, because both understanding[s] [by] divine usefulness advance[s] to salvation. for bread of life Christ is and bread this of all not is, but ours is. and how we say Father our, because of understanding and believing [ones] father he is, so also bread our we call, because Christ of those who body his we touch bread is. this [bread] however to be given [to] us daily we ask, lest [we] who in Christ are and eucharist his daily for food of salvation receive, intervening some heavier sin, while abstaining and not communicating from heavenly bread we are prohibited, from body of Christ we be separated [with] him himself preaching and saying: I am bread of life who from heaven I descended. if anyone will eat of my bread, he will live in eternity. bread however which I will have given flesh my is for of world life. when therefore he says in eternity to live if anyone will eat of his bread, as manifest it is [that] those live who body his touch and eucharist [by] right of communication receive, so on the contrary [it] is to be feared and to be prayed, lest while anyone abstaining is separated from body of Christ he remain away from salvation [with] him himself threatening and saying: unless you will eat flesh of son of man and you will drink blood his, not you will have life in you. and therefore bread our that is Christ to be given [to] us daily we ask, that [we] who in Christ remain and live from sanctification his and body not may depart.

choices.why: Uses the fixed glossary rendering for the petition's key term.
rejected: the bread we need each day

choices.why: Fixed glossary term; kept as 'Eucharist' rather than a paraphrase.
Preserves the legal force of 'iure' and the ecclesial sense of 'communicationis' as participation in the sacrament.
Keeps the two objects of 'recedamus' distinct and literal, matching the source's pairing.

choices.english: for the life of the world
choices.why: Literal rendering of 'saeculum' as 'world' in this Johannine context, preserving the gospel echo.
rejected: for the life of the age

pass_b_english: As the prayer continues, we ask and say: give us this day our daily bread. This can be understood both spiritually and simply, because each understanding serves our salvation by divine benefit. For Christ is the bread of life, and this bread is not everyone's, but ours. And just as we say our Father, because he is the Father of those who understand and believe, so we also call it our bread, because Christ is the bread of those of us who touch his body. We ask for this bread to be given to us daily, so that we who are in Christ and receive his Eucharist daily as the food of salvation may not, when some graver offense comes between, while abstaining and not communicating, be barred from the heavenly bread, and so be separated from Christ's body. He himself proclaims and says: I am the bread of life who came down from heaven. If anyone eats of my bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51). Therefore, when he says that whoever eats of his bread will live forever, it is clear that those who touch his body and receive the Eucharist by the right of communion live. So on the other hand we must fear and pray that no one, while abstaining, is separated from Christ's body, remains far from salvation, with him himself threatening and saying: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you (John 6:53). And so we ask for our bread, that is, Christ, to be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not withdraw from his sanctification and body.

problems.quote: through the intervention of some graver sin
problems.fix: when some graver offense comes between

problems.why: 'abstenti' means 'abstaining/refraining', not 'kept away'; 'non communicantes' is 'not receiving communion'.
problems.ruling: 'abstenti' = 'abstaining/refraining'; 'kept away' misrepresents voluntary abstention vs. passive exclusion.

problems.quote: by being kept away and separated
problems.why: 'abstentus' is 'abstaining', not passive 'kept away'; agency is self-imposed, not imposed.
problems.ruling: 'abstentus' = 'abstaining'; 'kept away' wrongly implies external restraint rather than self-imposed abstention.

problems.why: 'comminante' means 'threatening', not 'warning'; stronger, more urgent tone.
problems.fix: with him himself threatening and saying
problems.ruling: 'comminante' = 'threatening'; 'warns' loses the stronger, more urgent sense of divine threat.

edits.old: through the intervention of some graver sin
edits.new: when some graver offense comes between

edits.old: be kept away and barred from the heavenly bread while abstaining and not communicating
edits.new: while abstaining and not communicating, be barred from the heavenly bread

edits.old: by being kept away and separated from Christ's body
edits.new: while abstaining, is separated from Christ's body

edits.old: since he himself warns and says
edits.new: with him himself threatening and saying

fixed: Changed 'through the intervention of some graver sin' to 'when some graver offense comes between' to reflect 'intercedente aliquo grauiore delicto' (offense coming between, not intervention).

Changed 'kept away and barred... while abstaining and not communicating' to 'while abstaining and not communicating, be barred' to reflect 'abstenti et non communicantes' as self-imposed abstaining, not passive being kept away.
Changed 'by being kept away and separated' to 'while abstaining, is separated' to reflect 'dum quis abstentus separatur' as self-imposed abstaining.
Changed 'since he himself warns' to 'with him himself threatening' to reflect 'comminante ipso' (threatening, not warning).

problems.why: Latin 'contingimus' is first person plural ('we touch'), not third person.
problems.ruling: 'contingimus' is 1st person plural; 'those who touch' loses the 'we' meaning of the Latin verb.

edits.old: because Christ is the bread of those who touch his body
edits.new: because Christ is the bread of those of us who touch his body

fixed: Changed 'those who touch his body' to 'those of us who touch his body' because the Latin 'contingimus' is first person plural ('we touch'), not third person.

last_rejected.quote: because each understanding serves our salvation by divine benefit
last_rejected.source_quote: quia et uterque intellectus utilitate diuina proficit ad salutem
last_rejected.why: "utilitate diuina" means divine benefit/profit, but "proficit ad salutem" means profits/leads toward salvation, not "serves our salvation by divine benefit"
last_rejected.fix: because each understanding, by divine benefit, profits toward salvation
last_rejected.ruling: proficit ad salutem = 'profits toward salvation'; 'serves our salvation' is adequate paraphrase, not meaning change

last_rejected.quote: those of us who touch his body
last_rejected.why: Latin has "eorum... contingimus" (genitive plural + first person plural verb), meaning "of those who touch his body" where "we" are the ones touching; English "those of us who" changes the construction awkwardly but the "we" in "contingimus" is already the subject
last_rejected.fix: because Christ is the bread of those who touch his body
last_rejected.ruling: 'those of us who touch' captures eorum qui...contingimus; first person included naturally, no meaning lost

last_rejected.quote: when some graver offense comes between
last_rejected.why: "intercedente" means intervening/coming between, but "dum" (while) is missing; the Latin means "while some graver offense intervenes," not "when... comes between" as a temporal clause
last_rejected.ruling: 'when...comes between' renders dum...intercedente adequately; temporal/concessive nuance preserved

last_rejected.why: "comminante" is ablative absolute, not "with him threatening"; more importantly, "ipso" refers to Christ, but the English "with him himself" is garbled and unclear who threatens
last_rejected.ruling: 'with him himself threatening' correctly renders cominante ipso; ipso = Christ, clear from context

last_rejected.why: "remaneat a salute" means remains/keeps away from salvation, not "remains far from salvation"; "remaneat" is subjunctive of fear/prayer, "may remain away from"
last_rejected.ruling: 'remains far from salvation' adequately renders remaneat a salute; subjunctive fear context clear

last_rejected.source_quote: ego sum panis uitae qui de caelo descendi. si qui ederit de meo pane, uiuet in aeternum. panem autem quem ego dedero caro mea est pro saeculi uita
last_rejected.why: The citation John 6:51 is incorrect; this combines elements from John 6:48, 51, and 6:51b, but "pro saeculi uita" (for the life of the world/age) matches John 6:51b; however the full quotation spans multiple verses and should be cited as John 6:48-51 or similar
last_rejected.ruling: Citation John 6:51 covers core content; spanning 6:48-51 is preference, not error
